title: The Lost Patrol
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 15 of 40
content:
The dead left signals too.

Not strong ones. Not the kind that crossed states or summoned airships. Small emergency pings, weak enough to disappear beneath weather and radiation, repeating until a battery failed or someone finally came looking.

We went looking.

Recon Squad Artemis had vanished years before Gladius entered the Commonwealth. The Brotherhood knew pieces: a last route, scattered reports, nothing conclusive.

Danse took the search personally.

Of course he did.

We found the first body near an old training yard.

The holotag was still around the knight’s neck.

Danse knelt.

He did not know the man.

That did not matter.

He removed the tag carefully and closed the ruined armor plate over what remained.

“Ad Victoriam,” he said.

The words were quiet.

I waited until we were outside.

“What does it mean to you?”

“What?”

“Ad Victoriam.”

“To victory.”

“I know the translation.”

Danse adjusted his rifle sling.

“It means we don’t accept defeat.”

“Everyone gets defeated sometimes.”

“That’s not the point.”

“Then what is?”

He looked toward the next signal marker.

“That you keep moving toward the objective.”

Even when people died, I thought.

Especially then.

We found another member of Artemis at a satellite array. Super mutants had occupied the structure. Danse’s jaw tightened when we saw them, but he did not charge ahead.

He looked at me first.

“Two on the catwalk. One heavy weapon on the left.”

“Grenade through the lower window?”

“Too much chance of damaging the transmitter.”

“Roof access?”

“Better.”

We moved together.

After Fort Strong, that mattered.

He was listening.

So was I.

The fight ended with us crouched behind a ruined dish while bullets chewed through the railing.

Danse leaned close enough to be heard.

“On my mark, cross to the maintenance shed.”

“Together?”

“No. I’ll cover.”

“You always cover.”

“I’m wearing power armor.”

“That is not a personality trait.”

“It’s a tactical advantage.”

“Still.”

He looked at me.

For a second the battle disappeared from his face.

“Fine. You cover first.”

I smiled.

“Growth.”

“Shoot.”

I did.

We reached the signal source.

Another body.

Another holotag.

The recorded message was worse than the remains. A frightened voice reporting casualties, trying to reach command, promising to move east.

Danse listened without moving.

When it ended, he replayed the final ten seconds.

Then again.

“Danse.”

He shut it off.

“My squad could have ended like this.”

“Yes.”

“Haylen kept that transmitter alive with scrap and wire.”

“Yes.”

“Keane died the morning you arrived.”

“I know.”

He looked out through the broken wall.

“One day later, maybe you find three bodies in Cambridge instead of three people.”

The thought had occurred to me.

I had not wanted to give it words.

I touched his arm.

The metal was cool beneath my hand.

“But I didn’t.”

“No.”

“I found you.”

His helmet retracted.

His face held an expression I could not name.

“Yes,” he said. “You did.”

The final signal led us to a bunker.

Inside was Paladin Brandis, alive and half-feral with isolation.

He aimed a weapon at us.

Danse did not raise his own.

That mattered too.

He spoke carefully. Rank, name, proof. No threats. No contempt for a soldier who had broken under years alone.

When Brandis finally lowered the gun, Danse’s relief was visible.

Not every signal ended with a body.

We escorted him toward Brotherhood territory.

On the way, Brandis walked ahead.

I leaned toward Danse.

“You handled that well.”

“He’s a paladin.”

“He was pointing a gun at you.”

“He was scared.”

I looked at him.

Danse caught the look.

“What?”

“You knew that.”

“Obviously.”

“You’re better with people than you think.”

He nearly tripped over a chunk of concrete.

I pretended not to notice.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I’ve spent years giving orders.”

“That’s not what I mean.”

Brandis glanced back, forcing us to lower our voices.

Danse said, “You’re unusually determined to assign me virtues.”

“I’m unusually determined to assign you accuracy.”

“That sounds suspiciously familiar.”

“Learning from the best.”

His ears went faintly red.

By the time we reached the rendezvous, night had settled over the Commonwealth.

A Brotherhood team took Brandis aboard a vertibird.

Danse stood beneath the rotor wash with the recovered holotags in one hand.

Three signals answered.

One survivor.

“Victory?” I asked.

He looked at the tags.

“Not exactly.”

“Then what?”

He considered.

“Completion.”

That was honest.

I slipped my hand into his free one.

There were soldiers nearby.

This time Danse did not pull away.

He looked down at our joined hands, then at me.

“Off the record?” I asked.

His mouth softened.

“Off the record.”

The vertibird lifted.

We stood together until its lights disappeared.

The emergency beacon belonged to someone who had been waiting years for a rescue that came too late.

That was the cruelty of the Lost Patrol.

Each signal promised a living person until we reached it.

Each one gave us a body instead.

Danse became quieter with every tag we recovered.

At the second site, he knelt beside the remains of a Brotherhood knight and removed the holotag with both hands.

Not because it required two.

Because one would have looked casual.

“Do you know them?” I asked.

“No.”

He wiped dust from the metal anyway.

We followed the trail north.

By the time the final coordinates took us toward the old bunker, rain had begun to fall through the trees.

Danse checked the beacon receiver for the tenth time.

“You trust electronics less when they carry dead people,” I said.

He looked at me.

“I trust verification.”

“That too.”

Inside the bunker, the survivor met us with a weapon raised and years of grief packed into his voice.

Danse changed instantly.

He did not demand respect for his rank. He did not correct the man’s anger. He listened.

I watched him absorb every accusation about failed rescue, every detail of the patrol’s collapse, every name.

The survivor wanted to know where the Brotherhood had been.

Danse answered the question without hiding behind procedure.

“We didn’t know.”

It sounded inadequate because truth often does.

The man laughed bitterly.

“That supposed to make it better?”

“No.”

Danse’s voice stayed level.

“It’s supposed to be honest.”

That was the moment I understood why people followed him.

Not because he was always right.

Because when reality became ugly enough, he did not look away merely to protect his own authority.

We stayed longer than the mission required.

Danse helped repair the bunker generator. I sorted supplies. Neither of us called it charity.

When we finally stepped back into the rain, he carried the recovered tags inside a pouch against his chest instead of in the equipment case.

“You all right?” I asked.

“No.”

The answer stopped me.

Danse kept walking.

I caught up.

“That’s new.”

“What?”

“You answered the question.”

He glanced at me.

“You’ve made your opinion of ‘fine’ very clear.”

“I’m proud of you.”

“Don’t be patronizing.”

“I’m being sincere.”

“That’s worse.”

I smiled.

The rain strengthened. Danse moved closer so the bulk of his armor blocked some of it from hitting me.

He pretended this was accidental.

I pretended to believe him.

We delivered Artemis’ recovered holotags before leaving the rendezvous.

Danse made sure each one was logged separately. He corrected a scribe who tried to place the three tags into a single evidence pouch.

“They were individual soldiers,” he said.

The scribe immediately found three pouches.

Outside, I watched Brandis’ vertibird rise until it became a dark shape against the clouds.

“You think he’ll be all right?” I asked.

“I don’t know.”

The answer came easier than it once had.

“He survived three years alone,” Danse continued. “That kind of isolation changes a person.”

“You’re worried the Brotherhood will expect him to become who he was before.”

“Yes.”

“What do you expect?”

Danse thought about it.

“That he reports to medical. Sleeps. Eats something that isn’t bunker rations. Gets his equipment inspected.”

I waited.

His eyes narrowed.

“What?”

“That was the most Danse possible answer.”

“It’s practical.”

“It is.”

He looked back toward the sky. “And after that… I hope he finds a reason to stay.”

That was different.

Not duty.

A reason.

I filed the word away.

After a mile he said, “I keep thinking about Gladius.”

“I figured.”

“If someone had found them sooner…”

He stopped himself.

“Maybe,” I said.

“That isn’t helpful.”

“No. But pretending every death has a version where you personally could have prevented it isn’t helpful either.”

His jaw tightened.

“You don’t understand command.”

“No.”

The agreement surprised him.

“I understand loving people you can’t control.”

That landed.

Danse looked ahead through the rain.

Rain tapped against Danse’s armor in soft, irregular clicks.

For once he did not try to outwalk the thought.

“Brandis had three years to decide every death was his fault,” he said.

“And?”

“I nearly told him not to.”

“Why didn’t you?”

Danse looked at me.

“Because I realized I would not believe myself.”

That honesty hurt more than defensiveness would have.

“Maybe you don’t have to believe it all at once,” I said. “Maybe you just stop rehearsing the prosecution every night.”

His mouth twitched.

“That is a ridiculous metaphor.”

“You understood it.”

“Yes.”

After a long time, his hand opened between us.

Not reaching exactly.

Available.

I put mine into it.

Power armor made hand-holding ridiculous. His gauntlet could have swallowed my entire fist.

It was also strangely tender.

He kept hold of me all the way to the road.

ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
